Inherited from Old Hindi षट (ṣaṭa), from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀙 (cha), from Ashokan Prakrit *𑀙 (*cha), 𑀱 (ṣa), from Sanskrit षष् (ṣáṣ), from Proto-Indo-Aryan *ṣwáṭṣ, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *šwáćš, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs. Cognate with Marathi सहा (sahā), Gujarati છ (cha), Bengali ছয় (choẏ), Assamese ছয় (soy), Punjabi ਛੇ (che), and Nepali छ (cha).

From the same source as Punjabi ਛਿਤਰਨਾ /چھترانا (chitranā), Sindhi ڇِٽڙائِڻُ (chiṭṛāiṇu), Nepali छित्रिनु (chitrinu), Marathi शितडणे (śitaḍṇe). Turner reconstructs Old Indo-Aryan *छित्र- (*chitra-), as in *छित्रति (*chitrati) or *छित्रयति (*chitrayati). The Hindi and Nepali forms are either from Middle Indo-Aryan *छित्त- (chitta-) + Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀭- (-ra-) or borrowed from Northwestern Indo-Aryan where the Old Indo-Aryan rhotic is usually preserved. Platts instead suggests inheritance from Sanskrit क्षिप्त (kṣipta, “thrown”), from क्षिप् (kṣip). Note the existence of Prakrit 𑀙𑀺𑀢𑁆𑀢…
